title: 12. Cloud, Containers & Deployment: Disaster Recovery
summary: Disaster recovery (DR) is the set of policies, tools, and procedures that bring a system back online after a catastrophic failure — a region outage, a datacenter fire, a ransomware encryption, a bad deployment that corrupts…
objectives: Define RTO and RPO, and explain why they drive every DR architectural decision.
Compare backup-and-restore, pilot light, warm standby, and active-active. When would you choose each?
Why must backups be geographically separated and immutable, and what real incidents prove this?
What is a DR drill, and why are drills more important than the runbook itself?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Disaster recovery (DR) is the set of policies, tools, and procedures that bring a system back online after a catastrophic failure — a region outage, a datacenter fire, a ransomware encryption, a bad deployment that corrupts the database — measured primarily by two metrics: RTO (how fast you recover) and RPO (how much data you lose).
Every system will eventually fail in a way that single-AZ redundancy cannot survive. A region-wide AWS outage (2017 S3 in `us-east-1`, four hours; 2021 `us-east-1`, seven hours), a datacenter fire (OVHcloud Strasbourg in 2021, destroying one site and damaging another), a ransomware attack (Maersk in 2017, 49,000 endpoints encrypted and a 10-day rebuild), or a bad migration that drops a critical table — these are not theoretical risks but documented recurring events. Disaster recovery is the discipline of designing the system so that when one of these happens, you have a planned, tested, and bounded recovery path rather than an improvised scramble. The discipline is measured by two metrics that anchor every DR conversation. RTO (recovery time objective) is the maximum acceptable time between the failure and full service restoration — "we must be back online in 4 hours." RPO (recovery point objective) is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time — "we can afford to lose the last 15 minutes of writes, but no more." These two numbers drive every architectural choice: an RTO of 4 hours and an RPO of 15 minutes requires continuous replication; an RTO of 24 hours and an RPO of 24 hours can be satisfied with nightly backups.

The first concept is the four standard DR strategies, ranked by cost and recovery speed. The cheapest is "backup and restore": take nightly database backups to S3 (or equivalent), and on disaster, provision a new environment from scratch and restore the backup. RTO is typically 12–24 hours (provisioning, restoring terabytes), and RPO is up to 24 hours (whatever was written since the last backup). This costs almost nothing beyond the backup storage and is suitable for systems where downtime is tolerable — an internal reporting tool, a non-critical batch job. The next is "pilot light": keep a minimal version of the environment running in a second region — just the database, continuously replicated, with the app tier scaled to zero. On disaster, scale up the app tier and cut over. RTO is 1–4 hours, RPO is seconds to minutes, and cost is roughly 20–30% of full production. The next is "warm standby": a full but undersized replica of the environment in a second region, running continuously and replicating data, but not serving live traffic. On disaster, scale up the standby and shift DNS. RTO is 10–60 minutes, RPO is seconds, and cost is roughly 50–70% of full production. The most expensive is "multi-site active-active": both regions serve live traffic, and on disaster, the surviving region simply absorbs the failed region's load. RTO is minutes (DNS shift), RPO is seconds, and cost is 2× full production. The choice is a business decision driven by downtime cost and regulatory requirements.

The second concept is RTO and RPO in practice. RTO is not just "how long until the database is back" — it is the total elapsed time from failure detection to full service restoration, including detection (5–15 minutes for monitoring to alert and an engineer to acknowledge), decision (10–30 minutes for the incident call to confirm "yes, fail over"), execution (5–60 minutes for DNS, autoscaling, database promotion), and validation (15–60 minutes for smoke tests, traffic ramp, and confirmation). Real RTOs are often 2–4× the "happy path" RTO because the human and validation steps dominate. RPO is determined by the replication strategy: synchronous replication gives RPO=0, asynchronous gives RPO = replication lag (typically 1–5 seconds), nightly backups give RPO = time since last backup (up to 24 hours), and no backups at all give RPO = "all data since the system was created." The business must commit to specific RTO/RPO targets for each service tier: tier-1 (revenue-critical) might be RTO 1 hour, RPO 5 minutes; tier-2 (important) RTO 4 hours, RPO 1 hour; tier-3 (internal) RTO 24 hours, RPO 24 hours. These targets then drive the DR architecture for each tier.

The third concept is backups versus replication — they are not the same. Backups are point-in-time snapshots stored durably (S3, Glacier) and are the last line of defense against data corruption, accidental deletion, and ransomware (because the backup is offline and immutable). Replication is continuous copying of live data to another location and is the first line of defense against infrastructure failure (because the replica is already running and can be promoted). A robust DR strategy uses both: replication for fast failover (low RTO, low RPO) plus backups for recovery from logical corruption (an `UPDATE without WHERE` that replicates to all replicas but is caught and rolled back from a backup). The OVHcloud fire in 2021 destroyed a datacenter; customers who had only local backups (stored in the same site) lost everything, while customers with off-site backups or cross-region replication recovered. The 2017 Maersk NotPetya attack encrypted 49,000 endpoints and nearly all production data; the company was saved by a single off-site backup of one domain controller in a different country. The lesson is that backups must be geographically separated, immutable (WORM — write once, read many), and tested by actually restoring from them.

The fourth concept is DR drills — the practice of deliberately simulating a disaster to verify the recovery path works. Drills are necessary because DR systems decay silently: a standby database that has not been promoted in 6 months may have hidden replication lag, a DNS record's TTL may have been accidentally raised, a deployment may have updated the primary but not the standby, or an IAM role that failover depends on may have been deleted. The patterns are chaos engineering (Netflix's Simian Army randomly kills instances in production), regional failover tests (Netflix's Chaos Kong fails an entire region quarterly), table-top exercises (the team walks through a simulated disaster on a whiteboard), and full failover tests (actually shift traffic to the standby for a maintenance window). The discipline is what separates "we have a DR plan" from "we have a working DR plan." Without drills, the first real disaster reveals that the standby has been broken for months and the runbook is out of date; with drills, the team has muscle memory and the system has been proven. The cost of drills is operational (engineering time, brief user impact if the drill goes wrong); the cost of not drilling is a multi-hour or multi-day outage when a real disaster strikes.

The fifth concept is the recovery runbook — the document an on-call engineer follows during a disaster. The runbook must be specific enough that a stressed engineer at 3 AM can execute it without thinking, and it must be tested by someone other than its author (because the author's implicit knowledge is not in the document). A good runbook covers: detection criteria (what monitoring signal triggers the DR procedure), decision authority (who can declare a disaster and authorize failover — typically a senior engineer or manager, because failover has business cost), step-by-step execution (exact commands, with expected output and time estimates), validation (how to confirm the system is healthy after failover), and rollback (how to undo the failover if it makes things worse). The runbook must be version-controlled, linked from the on-call documentation, and reviewed quarterly. Real-world examples: AWS publishes detailed runbooks for region failover; Netflix's runbooks are integrated into their Spinnaker deployment system so the failover is a button, not a procedure; Google's Site Reliability Workbook devotes entire chapters to runbook design. The trade-off is that runbooks take time to write and maintain, but the alternative is a multi-hour outage while the team figures out what to do.

The sixth concept is the human and organizational side of DR. The technical architecture is necessary but not sufficient — disasters are won or lost by the people responding. The required organizational elements are: a defined incident commander role (one person makes decisions, others execute), an on-call rotation that ensures someone is always reachable, a communication plan (internal Slack channel, external status page, customer notifications), and a post-incident review process that produces action items (not blame). The 2017 AWS `us-east-1` outage was worsened because many customers had no runbook and engineers were improvising; the 2021 Facebook outage (6 hours, caused by a BGP misconfiguration that also took down the internal tools used to fix it) was extended because engineers could not reach the routers. The lesson is that DR must include the human path: who is called, how they communicate, what authority they have, and how they rehearse. DR drills are as much about training the people as testing the system. The trade-off summary: a complete DR posture costs roughly 20–100% more than single-region (depending on strategy), requires ongoing engineering investment (drills, runbook maintenance, replication monitoring), and delivers the ability to recover from catastrophic failure within a bounded, communicated time — which is increasingly a regulatory and customer expectation.

### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD Failure[Regional failure / corruption / ransomware] Failure --> Detect[Monitoring detects
5-15 min] Detect --> Decide[Incident call: declare disaster?
10-30 min] Decide -->|yes| Strategy{DR Strategy} Strategy -->|backup-restore| BR[Provision new env + restore backup
RTO 12-24h, RPO 24h] Strategy -->|pilot light| PL[Scale up app tier + promote DB
RTO 1-4h, RPO sec-min] Strategy -->|warm standby| WS[Scale standby + DNS shift
RTO 10-60min, RPO sec] Strategy -->|active-active| AA[DNS shift to surviving region
RTO min, RPO sec] BR --> Validate[Smoke tests + ramp traffic
15-60 min] PL --> Validate WS --> Validate AA --> Validate Validate --> Live[Service restored] Validate -.->|if worse| Rollback[Rollback failover] Rollback --> Decide Drill[Quarterly DR drill] -.->|proves path works| Strategy Drill -.->|trains team| Decide Backup[Off-site immutable backups] -.->|last-resort| BR ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` disaster strikes | v +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ | DETECT | | DECIDE | | EXECUTE | | monitor |--->| incident |--->| runbook | | alert | | commander | | step-by | | 5-15 min | | 10-30 min | | 5-60 min | +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----+-----+ | v +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ | VALIDATE | | RAMP | | LIVE | | smoke test|--->| 5%->100% |--->| service | | 15-60 min | | traffic | | restored | +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ total RTO = sum of all stages happy path: 35 min - 2h real world: 2-4x happy path (humans dominate) four DR strategies (cost vs recovery speed): backup-restore | $ | RTO 12-24h | RPO 24h pilot light | $$ | RTO 1-4h | RPO sec-min warm standby | $$$ | RTO 10-60m | RPO sec active-active | $$$$ | RTO min | RPO sec ``` ### Walkthrough 1. Monitoring detects the failure (region unreachable, error rate spiking, database corruption alert) and pages the on-call engineer, who acknowledges and declares an incident. 2. The incident commander decides to invoke the DR plan based on the runbook's criteria; the team executes the runbook step-by-step, choosing the strategy appropriate to the failure (regional outage = failover, corruption = restore from backup). 3. The team validates the recovery with smoke tests, ramps traffic from 5% to 100%, and confirms the system is healthy; if validation fails, they roll back and try a different strategy.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Disaster Recovery planner.
- Pick the cheapest strategy that meets the tier's RTO/RPO targets.
- Compute backup frequency and retention.
- Checklist of things that must be true for the strategy to work.
- Tier-based RTO/RPO targets (industry-standard ranges)
- Strategy characteristics: (name, rto_min, rpo_min, cost_multiplier)
- Regulated or global services need at least warm-standby
- RPO is 24h -> nightly backup, retain 30 days + monthly for 1 year

**Defines:** `ServiceProfile`, `pick_strategy()`, `backup_schedule()`, `prerequisites()`, `plan()`

```python
"""
Disaster Recovery planner.

Given a service's business-criticality and data characteristics,
computes:
  - the right DR strategy (backup-restore / pilot-light / warm-standby / active-active)
  - the required RTO and RPO targets
  - the backup schedule and retention
  - the approximate cost as a fraction of single-region production
  - a checklist of prerequisites that must be in place
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List

@dataclass
class ServiceProfile:
    name: str
    tier: int                 # 1 = revenue-critical, 2 = important, 3 = internal
    data_volume_gb: float
    write_rate_per_sec: int
    regulated: bool = False   # subject to compliance (e.g. financial, health)
    global_users: bool = False

# Tier-based RTO/RPO targets (industry-standard ranges)
TIER_TARGETS = {
    1: {"rto_min": 60,   "rpo_min": 5},     # tier-1: 1h RTO, 5min RPO
    2: {"rto_min": 240,  "rpo_min": 60},    # tier-2: 4h RTO, 1h RPO
    3: {"rto_min": 1440, "rpo_min": 1440},  # tier-3: 24h RTO, 24h RPO
}

# Strategy characteristics: (name, rto_min, rpo_min, cost_multiplier)
STRATEGIES = [
    ("backup-restore", 720,  1440, 1.05),
    ("pilot-light",      120, 1,    1.30),
    ("warm-standby",      30, 1,    1.70),
    ("active-active",      5, 1,    2.00),
]

def pick_strategy(profile: ServiceProfile) -> str:
    """Pick the cheapest strategy that meets the tier's RTO/RPO targets."""
    targets = TIER_TARGETS[profile.tier]
    # Regulated or global services need at least warm-standby
    if profile.regulated or profile.global_users:
        for name, rto, rpo, _ in STRATEGIES:
            if name in ("warm-standby", "active-active") \
               and rto <= targets["rto_min"] and rpo <= targets["rpo_min"]:
                return name
    for name, rto, rpo, _ in STRATEGIES:
        if rto <= targets["rto_min"] and rpo <= targets["rpo_min"]:
            return name
    return "active-active"  # fallback

def backup_schedule(profile: ServiceProfile, strategy: str) -> dict:
    """Compute backup frequency and retention."""
    if strategy == "backup-restore":
        # RPO is 24h -> nightly backup, retain 30 days + monthly for 1 year
        return {"frequency_hours": 24, "retention_days": 30,
                "monthly_snapshots": 12}
    if strategy == "pilot-light":
        # continuous replication + daily logical backup for corruption safety
        return {"frequency_hours": 24, "retention_days": 14,
                "continuous_replication": True}
    # warm-standby and active-active: replication + weekly logical backup
    return {"frequency_hours": 168, "retention_days": 30,
            "continuous_replication": True,
            "immutable_offsite": True}  # WORM bucket for ransomware safety

def prerequisites(strategy: str) -> List[str]:
    """Checklist of things that must be true for the strategy to work."""
    base = [
        "runbook version-controlled and reviewed quarterly",
        "on-call rotation with declared incident commander",
        "monitoring alerts on replication lag and failover readiness",
        "off-site immutable backups (WORM bucket in different region)",
    ]
    if strategy in ("pilot-light", "warm-standby", "active-active"):
        base += [
            "second region provisioned with Infrastructure as Code",
            "DNS TTL <= 60s on the failover record",
            "health check that fails fast (3 consecutive failures in 30s)",
            "standby database promotion tested in last 90 days",
        ]
    if strategy == "active-active":
        base += [
            "conflict resolution strategy defined (LWW / CRDT / app-merge)",
            "deployments roll identically to all regions",
            "quarterly Chaos-Kong-style full region failover drill",
        ]
    return base

def plan(profile: ServiceProfile) -> dict:
    strategy = pick_strategy(profile)
    targets = TIER_TARGETS[profile.tier]
    sched = backup_schedule(profile, strategy)
    cost_mult = next(c for n, _, _, c in STRATEGIES if n == strategy)
    return {
        "service": profile.name,
        "tier": profile.tier,
        "rto_target_min": targets["rto_min"],
        "rpo_target_min": targets["rpo_min"],
        "strategy": strategy,
        "cost_multiplier_vs_single_region": cost_mult,
        "backup_schedule": sched,
        "prerequisites": prerequisites(strategy),
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":
    services = [
        ServiceProfile("checkout-api",  tier=1, data_volume_gb=500,
                       write_rate_per_sec=2000, regulated=True),
        ServiceProfile("search-service", tier=2, data_volume_gb=2000,
                       write_rate_per_sec=100),
        ServiceProfile("internal-bi",    tier=3, data_volume_gb=5000,
                       write_rate_per_sec=5),
    ]
    for s in services:
        p = plan(s)
        print(f"\n== {p['service']} (tier {p['tier']}) ==")
        print(f"  strategy: {p['strategy']}")
        print(f"  RTO target: {p['rto_target_min']} min, RPO target: {p['rpo_target_min']} min")
        print(f"  cost: {p['cost_multiplier_vs_single_region']}x single-region")
        print(f"  backup: {p['backup_schedule']}")
        print(f"  prerequisites ({len(p['prerequisites'])}):")
        for item in p['prerequisites']:
            print(f"    - {item}")

# Expected output (abbreviated):
#   == checkout-api (tier 1) ==           strategy: warm-standby,  RTO 60,  RPO 5
#   == search-service (tier 2) ==         strategy: warm-standby,  RTO 240, RPO 60
#   == internal-bi (tier 3) ==            strategy: backup-restore,RTO 1440,RPO 1440
```

quiz.question: Define RTO and RPO, and explain why they drive every DR architectural decision.
options: The cost is latency: every write incurs the round-trip time between primary and standby, which for cross-region replication is 50–100 ms, devastating write throughput.
A DR drill is a scheduled exercise that deliberately simulates a disaster — killing instances, severing networks, failing a region — and observes whether the system actually recovers…

quiz.explanation: RTO (recovery time objective) is the maximum acceptable elapsed time between a failure and full service restoration — "we must be back online in 4 hours." RPO (recovery point objective) is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time — "we can lose the last 15 minutes of writes, but no more." These two numbers drive architecture because each DR strategy offers a specific (RTO, RPO) pair at a specific cost.

quiz.question: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous replication, and how does each affect RPO?
options: A DR drill is a scheduled exercise that deliberately simulates a disaster — killing instances, severing networks, failing a region — and observes whether the system actually recovers…
The incident commander (IC) is the single person who makes decisions during a disaster — declaring the incident, authorizing failover, coordinating the response — while others execute.
RTO (recovery time objective) is the maximum acceptable elapsed time between a failure and full service restoration — "we must be back online in 4 hours." RPO (recovery point objective)…
The cost is latency: every write incurs the round-trip time between primary and standby, which for cross-region replication is 50–100 ms, devastating write throughput.
quiz.explanation: Synchronous replication commits a write to both the primary and the standby before acknowledging the write to the client. The standby is guaranteed to have every committed write, so on failover no data is lost — RPO is zero. The cost is latency: every write incurs the round-trip time between primary and standby, which for cross-region replication is 50–100 ms, devastating write throughput.
